prompt: Your school is considering a phone-free policy during the school day. Write a text for school leaders in which you identify educational benefits and practical problems, recommend a workable policy, and explain how it should be introduced and reviewed.
requirements: Identify educational benefits and practical problems of a phone-free policy.
Explain how the policy should be introduced and reviewed.
textTypeRationale: A proposal is designed for decision-makers and naturally supports recommendations, implementation and review.
modelAnswerJa: 全面禁止か自由使用かの二択にせず、授業・休み時間・緊急連絡など場面別にルールを設計しています。Proposalの構成を使ってimplementationとreviewまで示しています。
modelAnswer:
Proposal: A Practical Phone Policy for the School Day

Purpose

This proposal recommends a school phone policy that reduces distraction during learning while recognizing that phones are also tools for communication, organization and, in some lessons, legitimate academic work.

Current problem

Teachers regularly report that notifications, messaging and social media interrupt concentration. Even when students do not actively use a phone, the temptation to check it can divide attention. Students also describe social pressure to respond immediately to messages during breaks. A clearer policy could therefore support both learning and wellbeing.

However, a complete ban would create practical difficulties. Some students use phones for translation, medical monitoring, transport information or communication with family after school. Teachers may also occasionally want students to use a device for research, photography or classroom activities.

Recommended policy

First, phones should be out of sight and silenced during lessons unless a teacher explicitly authorizes their use. This creates a simple default rule: no negotiation is needed at the beginning of every class, but teachers retain flexibility when technology genuinely supports learning.

Second, the school should create a limited number of phone-permitted areas during lunch. Students who need to check transport, contact family or manage an important message would have a clear place to do so. Other social spaces could remain phone-light to encourage face-to-face interaction.

Third, the policy should include reasonable exceptions. Students with documented medical or accessibility needs must be able to use devices when required. Emergency communication should go through the school office during lessons so that families know how to reach students without depending on personal messages.

Enforcement

Consequences should be predictable rather than dramatic. A first minor breach could lead to a reminder; repeated misuse could require the phone to be stored at the office until the end of the day. Staff should follow the same basic expectations about unnecessary personal phone use in front of students.

Implementation

The school should introduce the policy with a two-week preparation period. Students and parents should receive clear examples of permitted and non-permitted use. Teachers should also explain the learning reasons behind the policy instead of presenting it simply as a discipline measure.

Review

A one-term trial would allow the school to collect evidence. Teachers could report changes in classroom interruptions, while students could complete a short survey about concentration, communication and social pressure. The school should review exception requests and enforcement data to check whether particular groups are being affected unfairly.

Conclusion

The goal should not be to prove that phones are good or bad. The goal is to decide when they help and when they interfere. A clear default of phone-free lessons, combined with limited access, sensible exceptions and a formal review, would be more practical than either unrestricted use or an absolute ban.

prompt: You visited a public exhibition of new technologies designed to support people with disabilities. Write a text in which you evaluate the exhibition, discuss whether it presents technology as a complete solution or one part of accessibility, and recommend whether others should visit.
requirements: Evaluate strengths and weaknesses of the exhibition.
Discuss the relationship between technology and broader accessibility.
Give a clear recommendation to potential visitors.
audience: Potential visitors interested in technology and accessibility
purpose: Evaluate the exhibition and recommend whether it is worth visiting
textTypeRationale: A review combines description with judgment and a recommendation for prospective visitors.
modelAnswerJa: Technologyを称賛するだけでなく、cost・design・social barriersも扱い、exhibition自体のmessageを評価しています。Reviewとしてstrengths/weaknessesとrecommendationを明確にしています。
modelAnswer:
Review: Access by Design — Useful Technology, Better Questions

Technology exhibitions often promise that the future will solve problems the present has failed to solve. Access by Design, a new exhibition on assistive technology, is more careful. It presents impressive devices, but its strongest message is that accessibility depends on more than inventing clever tools.

The exhibition opens with practical technologies: screen readers, smart hearing devices, eye-tracking communication systems and lightweight robotic supports for people with limited mobility. Visitors can test simplified versions of several tools. This interactive approach is effective because it turns technical descriptions into understandable experiences without pretending that a short demonstration can reproduce another person’s disability.

One of the best sections focuses on design choices that benefit many users. A video explains how captions assist not only deaf viewers but also language learners and people watching in noisy places. Another display shows how step-free entrances support wheelchair users, parents with strollers and travellers carrying luggage. These examples make universal design feel practical rather than abstract.

The exhibition is also honest about limits. A device that costs thousands of dollars is not a complete accessibility solution if insurance, schools or public services cannot provide it. Similarly, perfect navigation software cannot help if a building has stairs but no lift. Technology can remove barriers, but laws, budgets, attitudes and physical design still determine whether people can participate.

I appreciated that disabled users were presented as designers and experts rather than simply as people receiving help. Short interviews describe how users modified early prototypes, rejected uncomfortable products and identified problems engineers had missed. This challenges the common idea that innovation always moves in one direction from inventor to user.

There are weaknesses. Some displays use too much technical vocabulary, and the section on artificial intelligence feels slightly overexcited. Facial and voice recognition tools are presented as promising, but privacy and bias receive only a small panel. Given how sensitive disability-related data can be, this deserved more attention.

The exhibition also risks creating inspiration moments in which visitors admire individuals for overcoming barriers instead of asking why those barriers exist. Fortunately, the final room addresses this directly by inviting visitors to redesign a public space rather than redesign a person.

Would I recommend the exhibition? Yes, especially for students interested in technology, design, health or social policy. Do not visit expecting a collection of futuristic gadgets. The real value is the argument behind the gadgets: accessibility improves when designers begin by listening to users and when society treats access as a shared responsibility.

Access by Design succeeds because it leaves visitors impressed by technology but not satisfied with technology alone. That is a more mature view of innovation, and a much more useful one.

prompt: Your school is worried about the spread of realistic AI-generated images and videos. Write a text for students in which you explain why deepfakes are difficult to judge, recommend habits for checking suspicious content, and persuade students not to share material simply because it is shocking or entertaining.
requirements: Explain why realistic AI-generated media can be difficult to judge.
Persuade students to pause before sharing suspicious content.
purpose: Build practical awareness about deepfakes and responsible sharing
register: Direct, clear and cautionary without being alarmist
textTypeRationale: A speech fits a school assembly and allows direct calls to action supported by concise explanation.
modelAnswerJa: 恐怖をあおるのではなく、具体的なverification stepsを提示しています。Assembly speechらしく短い問いかけとcall to actionを使っています。
modelAnswer:
Good morning everyone,

Imagine receiving a video that appears to show a famous politician making a shocking statement, or a classmate saying something offensive. Your first reaction might be anger, surprise or laughter. Now imagine discovering later that the video was created by artificial intelligence.

Realistic fake images, audio and video are not entirely new, but generative AI has made them easier to produce. This matters because our eyes and ears are used to being evidence. We often think, I saw it, so it happened. That assumption is becoming less reliable.

Deepfakes are difficult to judge for several reasons. First, quality is improving quickly. Advice such as look for strange hands or check whether the lips move correctly may help sometimes, but it is not a permanent solution. Second, fake content often reaches us in emotional situations. If a video confirms something we already believe, we are less likely to examine it carefully. Third, social media rewards speed. By the time a correction appears, the original post may already have been copied thousands of times.

So what should we do?

The first habit is simple: pause. If a piece of content makes you immediately furious or excited, that is exactly when you should slow down. Ask where it came from. Is the original source identifiable, or are you looking at a repost of a repost?

Second, check whether reliable organizations are reporting the same event. One video should not be the only evidence for an extraordinary claim. Search for the person, event and date using more than one credible source.

Third, look for context. A real video can still be misleading if it is edited, shortened or presented with a false caption. Verification is not only about asking, Was this generated by AI? It is also about asking, Is this being represented honestly?

Fourth, do not treat sharing as a neutral action. Adding I don’t know if this is real, but… does not remove responsibility. If you cannot verify material that could damage someone’s reputation or spread panic, the safest decision is often not to share it.

Some people will say this makes the internet less fun. Nobody wants to research every joke or harmless meme. The level of checking should match the possible harm. A ridiculous image of a cat wearing sunglasses is different from a video accusing a real person of a crime.

Schools also have a role. Media literacy should include practical examples of manipulated content, source checking and responsible use of AI tools. Punishment alone will not prepare students for a media environment in which fake and real material can look similar.

The goal is not to become suspicious of everything. It is to become slower, more careful and more willing to say, I don’t know yet.

Before you share shocking content, give truth a little more time than the algorithm wants you to.

Thank you.
